# Appendix {#sec-appendix .unnumbered}

## Further checks {#sec-further-checks .unnumbered}

These checks support the main text but are not needed to follow it, so they sit here.

### Question 1(b): a second method gives the same MaxBrShare {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| label: maxbrshare-second-method

# pmax() works across whole columns at once instead of one row at a time
max_pmax <- do.call(pmax, select(soap_raw, all_of(brand_cols)))
# Stops the render if the two methods ever disagree
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(soap$MaxBrShare, max_pmax)))
n_same <- sum(near(soap$MaxBrShare, max_pmax))
```

The vectorised `pmax()` gives the same value for all `r n_same` households (the `stopifnot()` check would stop the render otherwise). It is the more efficient form because it avoids creating a group for each row; `rowwise()` is kept above because it shows the row-by-row logic most clearly.

### Question 1(b): how concentration is spread {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| label: fig-q1b-maxbrshare
#| fig-cap: "Left: distribution of MaxBrShare. Right: MaxBrShare against the number of brands bought (line = median at each brand count)."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4

p_hist <- ggplot(soap, aes(MaxBrShare)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, boundary = 0, fill = pal[1],
                 colour = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(title = "Concentration on one named brand", x = "MaxBrShare",
       y = "Households")

p_scatter <- ggplot(soap, aes(NoBrands, MaxBrShare)) +
  geom_point(colour = pal[1], alpha = 0.7) +
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "line", colour = pal[2], linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(title = "More brands, less concentration", x = "Number of brands bought",
       y = "MaxBrShare")

p_hist + p_scatter
```

@fig-q1b-maxbrshare shows the spread. The middle half of households give between `r percent(quantile(soap$MaxBrShare, 0.25), accuracy = 1)` and `r percent(quantile(soap$MaxBrShare, 0.75), accuracy = 1)` of their volume to their favourite named brand, and `r sum(near(soap$MaxBrShare, 1))` give it all of their volume. Concentration falls as the number of brands rises, but households with the same brand count still differ widely, and the single-brand households include both 100% named-brand buyers and the zero group. This is why the two variables are read together.

### Question 1(b): do the nine shares add up to 1? {.unnumbered}

`r nrow(soap) - nrow(share_exceptions)` households have nine shares (eight named brands plus `BrOthers`) that sum to 1 within 0.01. The `r nrow(share_exceptions)` exceptions are shown in @tbl-q1b-share-exceptions. They are kept as supplied, because rescaling them would change the measure the question defines. Their `MaxBrShare` values are still valid shares between 0 and 1.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-q1b-share-exceptions
#| tbl-cap: "Households whose nine brand shares do not sum to 1 (share_exceptions from @sec-setup)."

share_exceptions |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(share_total, decimals = 3) |>
  cols_label(MemberID = "Household ID", share_total = "Sum of the nine shares")
```

### Question 2(e): where do the differences come from? {.unnumbered}

The tests above say *whether* the segments differ; this check says *which* segment and class cause it, so a client knows where to act. For SEC and AGE, the **standardised residual** of each cell compares the number of households in that segment and class with the number expected if every segment had the same mix. A value beyond ±2 marks a clear excess (positive) or shortfall (negative). For HS, **pairwise Wilcoxon tests** compare every pair of segments, with the **Holm adjustment** keeping the overall chance of a false difference at 5% across all the comparisons.

```{r}
#| label: fig-profile-residuals
#| fig-cap: "Standardised residuals of segment by SEC and by AGE. Beyond plus or minus 2 is a clear difference."
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.5

# Standardised residuals of the segment by class table, in long form for
# plotting
resid_df <- function(data, var) {
  d   <- data |> filter(!is.na(.data[[var]]))
  tab <- table(segment = d$segment, level = d[[var]])
  # Simulated p-value, so no small-cell warning; only the residuals are used
  res <- chisq.test(tab, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 2000)
  as.data.frame.table(res$stdres, responseName = "resid") |>
    mutate(variable = var)
}

plot_resid <- function(rd, title) {
  ggplot(rd, aes(level, fct_rev(segment), fill = resid)) +
    geom_tile(colour = "white") +
    geom_text(aes(label = round(resid, 1), colour = abs(resid) > 2),
              show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = pal_ink, `FALSE` = pal_ink)) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = pal[4], mid = "white", high = pal[1],
                         midpoint = 0) +
    labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Residual")
}

sec_resid <- resid_df(profile_df, "SEC")
age_resid <- resid_df(profile_df, "AGE")

plot_resid(sec_resid, "Socioeconomic class") +
  plot_resid(age_resid, "Age of the homemaker")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-profile-hs-pairs
#| tbl-cap: "Household size: segment pairs that still differ after the Holm adjustment."

hs_pairs <- pairwise.wilcox.test(hs_df$HS, hs_df$segment,
                                 p.adjust.method = "holm", exact = FALSE) |>
  tidy()

hs_pairs |>
  filter(p.value < 0.05) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(p.value, decimals = 4) |>
  cols_label(group1 = "Segment", group2 = "Compared with",
             p.value = "Holm-adjusted p-value")
```

```{r}
#| label: residual-values

resid_text <- \(seg, lvl) {
  sprintf("%+.1f",
          sec_resid$resid[sec_resid$segment == seg & sec_resid$level == lvl])
}
n_age_cells <- sum(abs(age_resid$resid) > 2)
```

@fig-profile-residuals and @tbl-profile-hs-pairs show the detail. The SEC result is driven by three segments: the Loyal promotion buyers have more SEC 4 households than expected (`r resid_text("Loyal promotion buyers", "4 Low")`), the Promo-6 buyers have more SEC 2 households (`r resid_text("Promo-6 buyers", "2")`), and the small Light occasional group has more SEC 1 households (`r resid_text("Light occasional buyers", "1 High")`). `r if (n_age_cells == 0) "No age cell goes beyond 2 in either direction, which matches the non-significant age test." else paste(n_age_cells, "age cells go beyond 2 in either direction, but the age test as a whole is not significant.")` For household size, only the pairs in the table above differ after adjustment, and every one of them involves the Heavy multi-brand shoppers' larger households. These are the comparisons a client should rely on when choosing which segment gets which offer.

### Question 2(e): did we miss a better demographic? {#sec-profile-check .unnumbered}

The three variables were chosen for business reasons. As a check, every demographic is measured on how strongly it separates the segments with one common measure, Cramér's V. Numeric variables (HS, Affluence and EDU, which has nine sparse levels) are first cut into four equal-sized groups, and native-language codes held by fewer than 20 households are pooled, so that rare codes do not inflate the measure.

```{r}
#| label: fig-profile-all-demographics
#| fig-cap: "How strongly each demographic separates the six segments (Cramer's V)."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5

all_demo_v <- map_dfr(demo_cols, \(v) {
  d <- soap_clusters |>
    select(MemberID, segment) |>
    left_join(soap_clean |> select(MemberID, value = all_of(v)),
              by = "MemberID") |>
    filter(!is.na(value))
  grp <- if (v %in% c("HS", "Affluence", "EDU")) {
    # numeric: four equal-sized groups
    factor(ntile(d$value, 4))
  } else {
    # categorical: pool rare codes
    fct_lump_min(factor(d$value), min = 20)
  }
  tab <- table(d$segment, grp)
  # Simulated p-value, so no small-cell warning; only the statistic is used
  res <- chisq.test(tab, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 2000)
  tibble(variable = v, n = nrow(d),
         cramers_v = cramers_v(tab, unname(res$statistic)),
         chosen = v %in% profile_vars)
})

all_demo_v |>
  ggplot(aes(cramers_v, fct_reorder(variable, cramers_v), fill = chosen)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = pal[1], `FALSE` = pal_grey),
                    labels = c(`TRUE` = "Chosen", `FALSE` = "Not chosen")) +
  labs(title = "How strongly each demographic separates the segments",
       x = "Cramer's V", y = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: check-values

demo_v <- \(v) round(all_demo_v$cramers_v[all_demo_v$variable == v], 3)
```

@fig-profile-all-demographics shows that every demographic separates the segments only weakly (the largest V is `r round(max(all_demo_v$cramers_v), 3)`), which repeats the finding above. HS and SEC are among the stronger variables, which supports two of the three choices. `Affluence` (V = `r demo_v("Affluence")`) and `EDU` (`r demo_v("EDU")`) separate the segments more than AGE (`r demo_v("AGE")`). They were left out because Affluence largely repeats SEC and EDU has many sparse levels and more missing values. Since the brief lets the team choose any three demographics, Affluence would be an acceptable alternative to AGE. It is reported here so a reader can see the trade-off rather than take the choice on trust.

## Packages used {.unnumbered}

@tbl-appendix-package-versions records the installed versions of every package explicitly loaded in the shared setup, together with the rendering dependencies. These versions are read from the R library at execution time, rather than transcribed from a previous run. The complete attached-package and namespace information follows in `sessionInfo()`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-appendix-package-versions
#| tbl-cap: "R packages loaded by the shared setup and dependencies used for rendering."

# Keep this list aligned with the explicit package calls in the shared setup.
appendix_packages <- tibble(
  package = c("pacman", "tidyverse", "tidymodels", "here", "janitor", "gt",
              "scales", "patchwork", "factoextra", "cluster", "moments",
              "mclust",
              "knitr", "rmarkdown", "ragg"),
  role = c(rep("Shared setup", 12), rep("Rendering", 3))
) |>
  mutate(version = purrr::map_chr(package,
                                  \(pkg) as.character(packageVersion(pkg))))

appendix_packages |>
  select(package, version, role) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(package = "Package", version = "Installed version",
             role = "Use in this report")
```

The table identifies the computational environment used for this particular render. Matching these versions helps another reader investigate differences between runs, although a version table alone does not install or lock dependencies. R and Quarto versions are recorded in @sec-reproduce.

## Session information {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| label: session-info

sessionInfo()
```

This output records the running R version, operating system, locale, attached packages and loaded namespaces. It supplements the explicit package table with dependencies loaded indirectly by the analysis.
